summary: Notes from a 1969 conversation with Bob Kahn about how the ARPANET's message processor handles things such as character code conversion and the fields used between a host and its IMP. It records ideas and suggestions rather than defining a protocol.

eli5.summary: Someone wrote down what they talked about with a colleague while working out how computers should pass messages, like notes from a chat about a team project.

subtitle: Notes from a 1969 discussion about character code conversion and Host-IMP communication.

tldr.problem: Different ARPANET hosts used different character encodings and had questions about how to handle code conversion transparently across the network.
tldr.mechanism: Steve Crocker documents a conversation with Bob Kahn from BBN about how IMPs can convert between character codes, what link fields should carry, and what status information flows between hosts and their IMPs.
tldr.outcome: This informal note captured early thinking about network architecture that fed into later protocol development. It records design questions that helped shape how the ARPANET handled heterogeneous systems.

today: This is a historical note from the very earliest days of ARPANET research. Later protocols like NCP and TCP adopted solutions to many of the issues Crocker and Kahn discussed. It survives as a record of how the network's architects thought about heterogeneity.

sections.title: Character Code Conversion
sections.content: The ARPANET connected hosts with different word sizes and character encodings. PDP-10 computers used 5 seven-bit ASCII characters packed into 36-bit words; IBM 360s used EBCDIC codes in 32-bit words. The conversation with Kahn discusses BBN's plan to convert all data to and from the standard NVT-ASCII format in the IMPs, with character code tables specific to each host. Crocker suggests that overflow from case shifting might be acceptable since it is rare.
sections.eli5: Some computers think words are 6-bit puzzles, others think they're 8-bit. The network agreement says 'everyone translate your puzzle to the standard shape, send it through, then translate back'.

sections.title: Host-IMP Protocol Details
sections.content: The note documents Host-to-IMP communication fields and signals: a 5-bit link field to identify the connection, a conversion bit, and status information. Hosts can send commands about tracing, conversion control, message destination, RFNMs (ready-for-next-message), host up/down status, synchronization, error format, and link clearing. IMPs respond with status on conversion, RFNM arrivals, IMP status, synchronization, host responsiveness, format errors, and internal state.
sections.eli5: A host tells its IMP what to do (trace this, convert that, is the host ready?) and the IMP tells back what happened (code converted, message ready, I am working).

sections.title: Historical Note
sections.content: This RFC is an informal working note, not a specification. It captures early ARPANET design discussions that informed later protocol work. It shows the practical concerns engineers faced when building the first packet-switched network connecting heterogeneous computers.
sections.eli5: This is not a rule book, just notes someone wrote down while working on a hard problem. It shows what people cared about in 1969.
